contradictions.question: Do rabbits chew their cud?
contradictions.summary: Leviticus 11:6 declares the hare unclean because it "cheweth the cud" but does not divide the hoof. The problem is that rabbits and hares simply do not chew cud. They are not ruminants. They lack the multi-chambered stomach that defines cud-chewing animals like cattle, sheep, and goats. The text places hares in a biological category they don't belong to.
contradictions.commentary: The apologist move here is what Gleason Archer pulls in the Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties — he points at cecotrophy. Rabbits eat their own soft fecal pellets, called cecotropes, to extract more nutrients on a second pass. Archer wants to call this "rumination" because it kind of looks like the animal is reprocessing food. That's the move. The problem is that it's not what rumination means in zoology and it's not what the Hebrew text is doing. The Hebrew phrase is *ma'alat gerah* — literally "bringing up the cud" — and the parallel verses (Leviticus 11:3-7, Deuteronomy 14:6-7) clearly group the hare with the camel and the rock badger as animals that "bring up" what's already been swallowed. Cecotrophy isn't bringing anything up. The pellets come out the back end. Mary Douglas in *Purity and Danger* and Jacob Milgrom in the Anchor Bible Leviticus commentary both treat this as a straightforward classification by the Israelite observer based on visible jaw motion — the constant chewing motion of hares and rock badgers looked like cud-chewing, so they got grouped that way. That is a perfectly reasonable thing for a Bronze Age priestly writer to do. It is not a perfectly reasonable thing for an omniscient deity to dictate. The harmonization only works if you redefine the Hebrew term to fit modern biology, which is the apologist playbook page one — read the text loosely enough and any error disappears. The text says the hare brings up cud. It doesn't.

contradictions.question: Can visual stimuli during conception affect the appearance of offspring?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 30:39 has Jacob's flocks conceiving in front of peeled striped rods and then producing striped and spotted lambs. The text is making a biological claim — that what an animal looks at while mating influences the genetics of its offspring. This is maternal impression theory, and it is not how heredity works. Coat patterns come from alleles, not from what mom was staring at.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologetic dodge here is to say God supernaturally produced the speckled offspring and Jacob's rods were just incidental — Walton in the IVP Bible Background Commentary leans this way. But that reading is a retrofit. The text gives no indication that the rods are decorative. Genesis 30:37-39 spells out a deliberate procedure: Jacob peels the rods, sets them in the watering troughs where the strongest animals come to drink and mate, and the flocks "conceived before the rods" and produced spotted offspring. The causal logic of the passage is that the visual exposure produced the phenotype. This is precisely the ancient Near Eastern folk belief in maternal impression — the idea that what a pregnant animal or woman saw could imprint on the fetus. It shows up in Pliny the Elder, in Soranus, in medieval bestiaries. Hermann Gunkel in his Genesis commentary identifies the rods explicitly as sympathetic magic, and Claus Westermann in the Continental Commentary treats it the same way. Even John Walton, who wants to preserve the historicity, admits this is operating on "ancient principles of animal husbandry" that are not scientifically valid. So the apologist has to choose: either the text means what it says and the biology is wrong, or the text is doing folklore and we shouldn't expect it to track modern genetics. Either way, the claim that visual stimuli at conception affects offspring is false, and the narrator of Genesis 30 presents it as if it works. That is of course a subjective reading of intent, but the syntax of verses 37-39 makes the causal chain hard to wave away.

contradictions.question: What is the shape of the earth?
contradictions.summary: Isaiah 40:22 describes God sitting upon the "circle of the earth," which apologists routinely cite as evidence the Bible knew the planet was spherical. Matthew 4:8 then has the devil taking Jesus up a mountain high enough to see "all the kingdoms of the world" — a geometry that only works on a flat earth. The contradiction is between a text apologists read as scientifically prescient and a text that assumes a flat-earth cosmology where altitude provides global visibility.
contradictions.commentary: First the Isaiah verse, because the apologetic case rests entirely on a translation move. The Hebrew word is *chug*, which means "circle" — a flat disc, a horizon line — not *kaddur*, which is the word for a ball or sphere (used in Isaiah 22:18). The standard critical commentaries — Brevard Childs in the OTL, Joseph Blenkinsopp in the Anchor Bible — all treat *chug* as describing a flat circular disc of land surrounded by waters, sitting under a domed firmament (*raqia*). That cosmology is everywhere in the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 1:6-8, Job 22:14, Job 38:13-14, Proverbs 8:27. It maps cleanly onto Mesopotamian flat-earth cosmology documented by Wayne Horowitz in *Mesopotamian Cosmic Geography*. So Isaiah 40:22 is not a spherical-earth verse. It is a flat-disc verse that some translations have made ambiguous in English. Now Matthew 4:8 — the temptation pericope. Davies and Allison in the ICC point out that the visual logic of "all the kingdoms of the world" being visible from a single mountain only makes sense in a worldview where the earth is flat enough that a high enough vantage point would show everything. Ulrich Luz in the Hermeneia volume agrees. The harmonization that the devil showed Jesus a vision is exactly the kind of post-hoc rationalization that has to be invented because the plain text doesn't work on a globe. The mountain in Matthew is a real mountain doing real geometry, and the geometry assumes a flat earth. Take your pick: either Isaiah 40:22 doesn't mean what apologists want it to mean, or Matthew 4:8 contradicts a sphere — most likely both.

contradictions.question: Do snakes eat dust?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 3:14 has Yahweh cursing the serpent to crawl on its belly and eat dust "all the days of thy life." Snakes do not eat dust. They eat rodents, eggs, birds, frogs, fish, and other snakes. The text makes a factual claim about reptilian diet that is false.
contradictions.commentary: Apologists run two harmonizations here and both fail. The first is the figurative reading — "eating dust" is just a Hebrew idiom for humiliation, like Micah 7:17 or Isaiah 65:25 or Psalm 72:9. That part is true. The phrase does function idiomatically elsewhere. The problem is that Genesis 3:14 is not just deploying a stock idiom. It is an etiology, a just-so story explaining why snakes look and move the way they do. The verse pairs "upon thy belly shalt thou go" — a physical description of legless locomotion — with "dust shalt thou eat," and the parallelism demands that both clauses be doing the same kind of work. If the belly clause is literal (and it has to be, since it explains the snake's anatomy), then the dust clause is too. Hermann Gunkel and Claus Westermann both read this as a classical etiological curse. Snakes flick their tongues to the ground constantly to taste-smell their environment, and an ancient observer easily concluded they were eating dirt. That is good ancient natural history. It is bad biology. The second harmonization, that snakes incidentally ingest some dust while striking prey, is grasping at straws — the text doesn't say snakes get a little dust on their food, it says dust IS their food, every day of their lives. John Walton in the NIVAC concedes that this is folkloric etiology and not zoological description. So the verse is making a factual claim about snake diet that doesn't comport with reality. The idiomatic reading rescues the metaphor at the cost of conceding the etiology — and the etiology is what the text is actually doing.

contradictions.question: How does the water cycle work according to the Bible?
contradictions.summary: This entry pairs Ecclesiastes 1:7 — rivers running to the sea and returning to their source — with Job 38:22, where snow and hail are kept in heavenly "treasuries" or storehouses. The pairing is meant to show the Bible has both a quasi-naturalistic hydrology and a mythological storehouse cosmology side by side, but the two verses are doing different things and aren't strictly contradictory on their own terms.
contradictions.commentary: This one is weaker as a contradiction than the database treats it. Ecclesiastes 1:7 is observational poetry — Qoheleth notes that rivers flow to the sea, the sea never overflows, and the cycle continues. That's not a precise hydrological cycle in the modern sense (no evaporation mechanism is described), but it's not making a false claim either. Job 38:22, by contrast, is straightforwardly mythological cosmology: snow and hail are stored in *otsarot* (storehouses or treasuries), the same kind of celestial reservoirs that show up in Deuteronomy 28:12, Jeremiah 10:13, and Psalm 135:7. Othmar Keel in *The Symbolism of the Biblical World* documents how this storehouse model maps to broader Ancient Near Eastern cosmology — Yahweh has chambers in the sky for rain, snow, hail, and wind. So the real tension is not between the two verses being compatible with each other but between Job's storehouse cosmology and modern meteorology. The Ecclesiastes verse is doing observational naturalism within an ANE worldview; the Job verse is doing mythological storehouse cosmology. They can coexist as different genres of Hebrew thought without strictly contradicting one another. The contradiction would be sharper if both verses were claiming to describe the same mechanism. As phrased, the question would be better recast as "Does the Bible reflect mythological cosmology about weather?" — at which point Job 38:22 alone does the work without needing Ecclesiastes 1:7 as a foil. That is of course a subjective call, but the entry as written conflates a non-contradiction with a real cosmological problem.

contradictions.prelim_flag: The two verses cited are doing different genres of work (observational poetry vs. mythological cosmology) and don't strictly contradict each other. The real cosmological problem is Job 38:22 alone vs. modern meteorology. Consider recasting the question or pairing Job 38:22 with a different verse.

contradictions.question: How many beatitudes are in the Sermon on the Mount?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:3-11 lists nine separate "blessed are" statements as part of the Sermon on the Mount. Luke 6:20-23, in the parallel Sermon on the Plain, lists only four. The two accounts diverge sharply both in number and in content — Luke's beatitudes are addressed in the second person to the materially poor and hungry, while Matthew spiritualizes them ("poor in spirit," "hunger and thirst after righteousness") and addresses them in the third person.
contradictions.commentary: The harmonization apologists like Blomberg deploy is that Matthew and Luke are reporting different sermons on different occasions, so the numerical difference doesn't matter. Two sermons, two sets of beatitudes, no contradiction. The Synoptic data does not support this. Both sermons follow the same narrative position in their respective Gospels (after the calling of disciples, before the healing of the centurion's servant), share the same core sayings about the poor, the hungry, and the persecuted, and conclude with the same parable about building on rock versus sand. Critical scholarship from Hans Dieter Betz to Ulrich Luz to Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Luke treats these as two redactional reworkings of a common Q tradition. Matthew has expanded the list by adding the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers, and has spiritualized the social-economic categories — "poor" becomes "poor in spirit," "hungry" becomes "hungering for righteousness." Luke has preserved a sharper, more economically literal version closer to Q. This is the Synoptic Problem at work — the same source material gets reshaped by each evangelist to serve their theological purpose. So the question "how many beatitudes are in the Sermon" only generates a contradiction if you assume the two Gospels are giving independent eyewitness reports of the same event. Once you accept that both are literary compositions drawing on shared earlier tradition, the divergence is exactly what source-critical scholarship predicts. The apologist needs the two-sermon theory to preserve inerrancy, but the parallels are too tight and the redactional fingerprints too obvious. Matthew added beatitudes. Luke kept fewer. Take your pick on which one matches what Jesus actually said.

contradictions.question: Who prophesied about the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 27:9 attributes the quotation about the thirty pieces of silver to Jeremiah the prophet. The actual quotation comes from Zechariah 11:12-13, not Jeremiah. Jeremiah has nothing about thirty pieces of silver — the closest material is the potter's house and the field-purchase narrative in Jeremiah 18-19 and 32, but the specific wording Matthew quotes is unambiguously Zecharian.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the most discussed citation problems in the New Testament. The apologetic responses cluster around three moves and none of them hold up cleanly. Move one, from Gleason Archer and others, is that Matthew is conflating Jeremiah and Zechariah and intentionally citing the more prominent prophet — there's a rabbinic convention of citing a composite quote under the better-known name. This is the strongest harmonization, and Davies and Allison in the ICC give it serious attention. The problem is that the Matthean citation doesn't actually fuse two passages — it quotes Zechariah and attaches Jeremiah's name. There's no Jeremiah material in the quoted text. Move two is that Matthew is alluding to Jeremiah 19 (the potter's flask, the bloody field) and Jeremiah 32 (the field purchase for silver) thematically while quoting Zechariah's wording. This works as a typological reading but doesn't explain why Matthew names Jeremiah as the source of the quote, not just the theme. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* concludes the most likely explanation is straightforward — Matthew or his source made a mistake. Move three is the textual-variant dodge, citing the few late manuscripts that read "Zechariah" or omit the name, but Bruce Metzger's *Textual Commentary* makes clear that "Jeremiah" is the original reading, and the variants are scribal corrections of the embarrassment. So the apologist is left with: either Matthew made a citation error, or he was using a non-canonical Jeremianic tradition that no longer exists, or he's doing some rabbinic conflation that the text doesn't actually support. The simplest reading — Matthew misattributed Zechariah to Jeremiah — is the parsimonious one.

contradictions.question: Should you answer a fool according to his folly?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs 26:4 says do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him. The very next verse, Proverbs 26:5, says answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes. The two verses give directly opposite instructions using nearly identical wording, juxtaposed back-to-back in the same chapter.
contradictions.commentary: This is the classic example of a deliberately paired contradiction in wisdom literature, and the apologetic response is actually pretty good — but it concedes more than apologists usually admit. The standard harmonization, articulated by Bruce Waltke in the NICOT Proverbs commentary and by Michael Fox in the Anchor Bible, is that the two verses are a deliberate juxtaposition meant to signal the situational nature of wisdom. Sometimes engaging a fool drags you down to his level; sometimes refusing to engage leaves him puffed up. The wise person discerns which situation calls for which response. That is a perfectly defensible reading. It's also a reading that admits the surface contradiction is real and intentional — the editors of Proverbs placed these two verses next to each other precisely because they don't agree, and the disagreement itself is the lesson. So this is not really a contradiction in the inerrantist sense; it's a feature of wisdom literature that resists systematization. The problem for apologists is that this same hermeneutic — "the contradiction is the point" — can't easily be transported elsewhere. When Matthew and Mark disagree about the time of the crucifixion or about who Jesus appeared to first, you don't get to say "the contradiction is the point, it teaches us about the situational nature of truth." Proverbs 26:4-5 works because it's an explicit pedagogical pairing. So as a contradiction this entry is technically valid on the surface but rhetorically weak — the resolution is right there in the literary form. The honest verdict: real surface tension, intentional editorial juxtaposition, and the resolution is genre-internal.

contradictions.question: How many apostles were in office between the resurrection and ascension?
contradictions.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:5 reports that the risen Jesus appeared "to Cephas, then to the twelve." But by the time of the resurrection, Judas Iscariot had already died (Matthew 27:3-5), and Matthew 28:16 explicitly calls the post-resurrection group "the eleven disciples." Acts 1:9 has Jesus ascending while the eleven look on, and Matthias is not selected until Acts 1:26. So between resurrection and ascension the apostolic college numbered eleven, not twelve.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic move here is to say "the twelve" is a titular collective name for the apostolic group — like calling a sports team "the Bulls" even when one player is injured. Anthony Thiselton in the NIGTC 1 Corinthians commentary and Gordon Fee in the NICNT both adopt this reading: "the twelve" functions as a fixed designation for the apostolic body regardless of actual membership. That's a defensible reading and it's probably what Paul means. But it doesn't fully dissolve the tension — Paul is reporting a resurrection appearance, presumably with a specific historical referent, and at the moment of that appearance the group physically present numbered eleven men. The standard critical observation, made by Hans Conzelmann in the Hermeneia 1 Corinthians, is that Paul is quoting an early creedal formula (1 Corinthians 15:3-5) that pre-dates his letter. The formula's use of "the twelve" probably reflects pre-Pauline tradition that hadn't yet been harmonized with the Judas-betrayal narrative. There's an even deeper problem: the textual variants. Some witnesses read "the eleven" instead of "the twelve" in 1 Corinthians 15:5 — Bruce Metzger's *Textual Commentary* discusses this. The fact that scribes felt the need to correct the number to eleven shows that ancient readers also saw the conflict. So either Paul (or his pre-formed creed) is using "the twelve" as a fixed title that doesn't track actual headcount, or there's an unresolved tension between the Pauline tradition and the gospel narratives about Judas. The titular reading is defensible but it concedes that the number is not literal — which means the contradiction is real at the level of arithmetic and only dissolves at the level of conventional usage.

contradictions.question: Should Christians judge others?
contradictions.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 2:15 says the spiritual person "judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man." Two chapters later in the same letter, 1 Corinthians 4:5, he tells the same audience to "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come." The two verses use related Greek verbs from the same root (*anakrinō* in 2:15, *krinō* in 4:5) and address the same community on the same general topic, and they push in opposite directions.
contradictions.commentary: This is the kind of contradiction that actually has a decent contextual resolution, but the resolution requires admitting that Paul is using *krinō* in two different senses, which is fine but undermines the inerrantist insistence on consistent semantic usage. In 1 Corinthians 2:15, the verb *anakrinō* (to examine, discern, evaluate) describes the pneumatic person's capacity to discern spiritual realities — it's the same word used in Acts 17:11 of the Bereans examining the scriptures. In 1 Corinthians 4:5, the verb *krinō* describes premature verdict-rendering, particularly about whether Paul and Apollos are faithful ministers. So Paul is saying: discern things now, but don't pronounce final judgment until the eschaton. Anthony Thiselton and Gordon Fee both handle this in their commentaries by mapping the semantic range of *krinō* across Paul's usage. The harmonization works, but only if you accept that "judge" doesn't mean one consistent thing — and inerrancy as commonly defended depends on the text speaking with semantic precision. The broader Pauline corpus is even messier. Romans 14:4 tells believers not to judge each other's diet practices; 1 Corinthians 5:12 tells believers to judge insiders; 1 Corinthians 6:2-3 says the saints will judge angels. Paul is not operating with a single doctrine of judgment. He's operating contextually, which is fine if you read him as a pastoral letter-writer responding to specific situations, and a problem if you read him as the inspired and consistent author of a unified systematic theology. So the contradiction is real at the lexical surface and softens with contextual analysis — but the harmonization concedes that Paul is using overlapping vocabulary inconsistently across contexts.

contradictions.question: How long was Jesus in the tomb?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 12:40 has Jesus predicting he will be "three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" — a precise duration of 72 hours, paralleling Jonah in the fish. But the passion narratives uniformly have Jesus crucified Friday afternoon (the day of preparation) and discovered risen Sunday morning. That's at most two nights (Friday night, Saturday night) and parts of three days. The arithmetic doesn't get to three nights.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the harder ones for apologists because the numbers just don't work. The standard harmonization, from Gleason Archer and Craig Blomberg, invokes the rabbinic principle of inclusive reckoning — any part of a day counts as a whole day. So Friday (part) + Saturday + Sunday (part) = three days. The Talmud Yerushalmi Shabbat 9:3 is cited in support. The problem is that the principle covers days, not nights. "Three days" with inclusive reckoning gets you Friday-Saturday-Sunday. "Three nights" with inclusive reckoning gets you... Friday night and Saturday night. Two. There is no third night. You can't include Thursday night because Jesus wasn't dead yet, and you can't include Sunday night because he was already risen. Matthew 12:40 specifically pairs days with nights — three of each — and the Jonah parallel makes the parallelism load-bearing. R. T. France in the NICNT Matthew tries to argue that "three days and three nights" is itself an idiom for a span of time including any part of three days, but he admits the case is strained. Some apologists try to rescue the count by moving the crucifixion to Wednesday — the "Wednesday crucifixion" theory — but this requires rewriting the chronology of the entire passion week against the unanimous testimony of the four gospels that the day of preparation was the day before the Sabbath. So the apologist has three options: redefine "three days and three nights" as a non-literal idiom (which deflates Matthew 12:40's deliberate parallel with Jonah), invent a Wednesday crucifixion (which the gospels don't support), or admit that Matthew 12:40 is overshooting the actual chronology. Take your pick. The parsimonious reading is that Matthew is enhancing the Jonah typology and the result doesn't precisely match the synoptic chronology of the passion.

contradictions.question: Does God give freely or withhold his blessings?
contradictions.summary: James 1:5 and Luke 11:10 present God as giving freely and liberally to all who ask. But John 12:40 (quoting Isaiah 6:10) has God blinding eyes and hardening hearts so people cannot be converted; Joshua 11:20 says it was "of the LORD to harden their hearts" so they would fight Israel and be destroyed; and Isaiah 63:17 has the prophet accusing God of making his people "err from thy ways" and hardening their hearts. The contradiction is between God-as-generous-giver and God-as-active-spoiler-of-salvation.
contradictions.commentary: This is the Calvinist-Arminian fault line written into the canon itself. Apologists usually run two harmonizations. The first is the theodicy move — God hardens hearts only after the recipients have already hardened their own (cf. Romans 9:18 with the Pharaoh narrative as the test case). On this reading, divine hardening is judicial: God ratifies a prior human choice. Walter Brueggemann in the OTL Isaiah 40-66 commentary, and Douglas Moo in the NICNT Romans, both engage this seriously. The problem is that the texts don't actually support the "prior hardening" sequence consistently. Joshua 11:20 has the Canaanites hardened *so that* God can destroy them — the purpose is annihilation, and there's no indication of prior moral choice driving the divine action. Isaiah 63:17 has the prophet accusing God directly: "Why hast thou made us to err?" — this is not a recipient who hardened first. John 12:40, quoting Isaiah 6:10, makes the hardening the cause, not the consequence, of the people's failure to believe — the verse explicitly says God blinded and hardened them "that they should not see... and be converted, and I should heal them." The second harmonization, the Calvinist one, just bites the bullet: God sovereignly chooses to give to some and harden others, and James 1:5 applies only to the elect. This preserves consistency at the cost of making "giveth to all liberally" mean "giveth to the elect liberally," which is a meaningful narrowing the text doesn't perform on its own. So the apologist is stuck: either God's generosity is genuinely universal (in which case the hardening texts contradict it) or it's restricted (in which case James and Luke are speaking imprecisely). The contradiction is real and it runs through the canon's competing soteriologies.

contradictions.question: Is God to be found by those who seek him?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 7:8 and Proverbs 8:17 both promise that those who seek will find — the seeker-finds-God formula is presented as a universal principle. Proverbs 1:28 directly contradicts it: "Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me." The same wisdom tradition that promises finding also promises non-finding under certain conditions.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic harmonization is straightforward and partially defensible: Proverbs 1:28 is the voice of personified Wisdom rejecting those who previously rejected her — it's a context-specific judgment on those who scorned wisdom when she called. Bruce Waltke and Michael Fox both read it this way. So the contradiction is contextual, not absolute. Fair enough. But this resolution does some work for the apologist and some work against them. It resolves the surface contradiction by saying "seek and you shall find" comes with an implicit time limit — you have to seek before you've definitively rejected wisdom, after which the door closes. That's a coherent doctrine. The problem is that Matthew 7:8 doesn't include the time limit. Jesus's framing is unconditional: "every one that asketh receiveth." *Pas* — every. Not "every one who has not previously rejected," not "every one within the window." If the apologist imports Proverbs 1:28's time-limit qualifier into Matthew 7:8, they're harmonizing by inserting a condition the text doesn't state. If they don't, then Matthew 7:8 and Proverbs 1:28 are making incompatible promises. Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in the ICC point out that Matthew 7:7-8 sits within a sermon that promises confidence in prayer without qualification — and Matthew's larger context, particularly the rejection of the Pharisees in chapters 23 and the apocalyptic discourse, does include conditions for being shut out. So even within Matthew the universal promise gets qualified elsewhere. The real verdict: there is an absolute-sounding promise in Matthew 7:8 and a conditional non-promise in Proverbs 1:28, and the texts achieve consistency only when readers smuggle each verse's qualifications into the other.

contradictions.question: Does God destroy man for his wickedness?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 6:5-7 has God resolving to destroy humanity precisely because "the wickedness of man was great" and "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually." After the flood, Genesis 8:21 has the same God promising never again to curse the ground or smite all living things for man's sake — and giving as his reason "for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." The exact same reason that motivated the flood is now cited as a reason NOT to flood again.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleaner contradictions in Genesis because the same Hebrew phrase — *yetser libbo ra* (the inclination of his heart is evil) — appears in both verses, and it functions as the explicit grounds for opposite divine decisions. In Genesis 6:5 the evil inclination triggers destruction; in Genesis 8:21 it triggers forbearance. Apologists like Kenneth Mathews in the NAC Genesis volume try to harmonize by saying that 8:21 reflects God's mercy responding to Noah's sacrifice — the post-flood promise is a new covenantal move that doesn't contradict the pre-flood judgment because circumstances have changed. That works narratively but it doesn't dissolve the contradiction in the divine reasoning. The text doesn't say "because of Noah's sacrifice I will hold back." It says "because man's heart is evil from his youth I will hold back" — using the evil inclination as the *reason for restraint*. This is one of the strongest pieces of source-critical evidence for the JEDP hypothesis. Critical scholars from Hermann Gunkel to Claus Westermann to Joel Baden have noted that Genesis 6 and Genesis 8 carry different sources within the flood narrative — Genesis 6:5-8 is widely assigned to J (the Yahwist), and so is Genesis 8:20-22. So the contradiction is internal to a single source, not just an artifact of redaction. Robert Alter handles this by reading the divine character development across the narrative — God learns that destruction doesn't fix the human condition and resolves on a different strategy. That's a literary reading and it has real merit, but it concedes that God in Genesis 8:21 is not the immutable God of later systematic theology. He's a deity who changes his mind in response to experience. Either the deity learns and changes (which contradicts immutability) or the text contradicts itself about the relationship between human evil and divine destruction. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Can God's attributes be known?
contradictions.summary: Paul in Romans 1:20 says God's invisible attributes — his eternal power and divine nature — are "clearly seen" from the creation, so that humans are "without excuse." Job 11:7 has Zophar asking "Canst thou by searching find out God? Canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?" — the implied answer being no. Isaiah 40:28 says of God "there is no searching of his understanding." The contradiction is between Paul's claim that God's nature is plainly accessible through observation of creation and the wisdom-tradition claim that God is fundamentally beyond human search.
contradictions.commentary: This one softens significantly once you parse what each text is actually claiming. Paul in Romans 1:20 is making a specific argument about *general revelation* — the existence of God and his power are evident from creation, which is enough to render Gentiles morally culpable. He's not claiming that the full divine nature is exhaustively knowable. Joseph Fitzmyer in the Anchor Bible Romans points out that Paul's argument has a polemical purpose: stripping Gentiles of the excuse of ignorance. Job 11:7 and Isaiah 40:28 are making a different claim — that God's *full* nature, his unsearchable understanding, his perfect knowability, exceeds human capacity. Both could be true at once: God's existence and power are evident, but his complete nature is unsearchable. Most apologists run this distinction and most critical scholars accept it. So the surface contradiction has a real exegetical resolution. The remaining problem is that Romans 1:20 has been historically deployed by apologists as much more than a minimal-knowability claim — it's used to argue that natural theology can deliver substantive attributes of God (omniscience, omnipotence, eternality, moral character) directly from observation of nature. That stronger reading does conflict with Job and Isaiah. So the contradiction is real if Romans 1:20 is read maximally and dissolves if it's read minimally. The standard exegesis goes minimal. The popular apologetic deployment goes maximal. That is of course a subjective call about the use rather than the text — but as a textual contradiction this entry is weaker than it looks. The verses can be reconciled by carefully delimiting what "knowing God" means in each context.

contradictions.question: Should the blood-shedder be put to death?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 9:5-6 lays down the Noahide blood-vengeance principle: whoever sheds human blood, by man shall his blood be shed, because humans are made in God's image. This is presented as a universal post-flood law. Genesis 4:15 has God explicitly protecting Cain — the original murderer — from being killed, marking him so no one will kill him, and threatening sevenfold vengeance on anyone who does. God's policy toward blood-shedders is opposite in the two passages.
contradictions.commentary: The standard harmonization is chronological: Genesis 9:5-6 establishes the death penalty post-flood, while Genesis 4:15 reflects a pre-flood, pre-law dispensation when the formal mandate for capital punishment hadn't yet been given. Kenneth Mathews and Wenham both run this version. That's a coherent narrative reading and it does dissolve the contradiction on a flat-chronological reading of Genesis. The problem is that the canonical-chronological reading is exactly the kind of harmonization that source criticism dismantles. Critical scholars from Gunkel through Westermann through Joel Baden assign Genesis 4:15 to J (the Yahwist) and Genesis 9:5-6 to P (the Priestly source). They reflect different theological visions of how God deals with murderers. The J source preserves an older tradition where Cain is protected even after fratricide — the mark of Cain is apotropaic, designed to keep blood vengeance from spiraling. The P source articulates the later legal principle that bloodshed requires bloodshed because of the image-of-God theology that P develops elsewhere (Genesis 1:26-27). So the contradiction is not just narrative; it's theological, reflecting two different streams of tradition about divine justice. Apologists who run the chronological harmonization implicitly concede that God's policy toward murder changed between Cain and Noah, which raises a separate theological problem — if the death penalty for murder is grounded in the image of God (Genesis 9:6), and humans were made in God's image from the start (Genesis 1:27), then the principle was always operative and Cain's protection was an arbitrary divine exception. The image-grounded reasoning of 9:6 makes the chronological harmonization sit awkwardly with the broader Priestly anthropology. Either policy changed, or two sources disagree, or both. The contradiction is real and the harmonization carries theological costs.

contradictions.question: Is improvidence okay?
contradictions.summary: Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount and parallel Lukan material tells his followers to take no thought for tomorrow, to give to everyone who asks, to lend without expecting return, and to consider the lilies of the field who neither toil nor spin. 1 Timothy 5:8 condemns anyone who fails to provide for his own household as "worse than an infidel," and Proverbs 13:22 praises the good man who leaves an inheritance to his children's children. Improvidence is celebrated in Matthew/Luke and condemned in the Pastoral Epistles and Proverbs.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic move here is to spiritualize the synoptic material as eschatological or attitudinal rather than economic. Don Carson and Craig Keener both argue that "take no thought for the morrow" doesn't mean "don't plan" — it means "don't be anxious," the verb *merimnaō* carrying the sense of crippling worry rather than prudent provision. On that reading, Jesus isn't condemning planning, just anxiety, and 1 Timothy 5:8 is perfectly compatible. This is a defensible exegesis and probably catches part of what Matthew is doing. But it concedes a lot. The radical sayings of Jesus in Matthew 6 and Luke 6 are framed in language that goes well beyond "just don't be anxious." "Sell your possessions and give alms" (Luke 12:33), "give to every one that asketh of thee" (Luke 6:30), "lend, hoping for nothing again" (Luke 6:35) — these are not anxiety-management instructions, they are concrete economic practices. Pieter Craffert and other social-scientific NT scholars have documented that the historical Jesus movement appears to have practiced a radical itinerant economic ethic at odds with householder values. The Pastoral Epistles — almost certainly pseudonymous on the consensus of critical scholars from Bart Ehrman to Margaret MacDonald — represent a later, settled Christian community institutionalizing household and inheritance norms. So the contradiction reflects a real diachronic shift: the early radical Jesus tradition demanded improvidence as a form of trust in eschatological provision; the later church needed stable households and economic responsibility. Ehrman in *Forged* and Raymond Collins in the Sacra Pagina Pastorals both treat 1 Timothy as second-generation Christianity adjusting Jesus's economic ethics for ongoing community life. The harmonization works only if you read Jesus's radical sayings as hyperbole and the Pastorals as their plain meaning — at which point you're picking which texts speak literally. The development is real, and reading it as a contradiction is honest historiography.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to get angry?
contradictions.summary: Ephesians 4:26 says "Be ye angry, and sin not" — anger is permitted, even commanded, as long as it doesn't lead to sin and isn't carried into the next day. Ecclesiastes 7:9 warns against being hasty to anger because "anger resteth in the bosom of fools." Proverbs 22:24 warns against even associating with an angry man. James 1:20 says "the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God." The texts pull in opposite directions on the moral status of human anger.
contradictions.commentary: This one has a relatively clean exegetical resolution that works for most of the texts but leaves residual tension. Ephesians 4:26 is quoting Psalm 4:4 (LXX *orgizesthe kai mē hamartanete*) and almost certainly means something like "in your anger, do not sin" — it's not actually commanding anger, it's regulating it. So even at the lexical level, the Ephesians verse is closer to "when you find yourselves angry, don't let it become sin" than to a positive endorsement of anger. Andrew Lincoln in the WBC Ephesians and Harold Hoehner both read it this way. That brings Ephesians 4:26 closer to the Ecclesiastes/Proverbs/James pole than the contradiction suggests. The remaining tension is genuine but smaller — the wisdom tradition and James present anger as basically negative, while Ephesians 4:26 acknowledges anger as a feature of human experience that must be managed rather than purely condemned. That's a difference of emphasis, not a flat contradiction. Where the contradiction sharpens is in the broader biblical treatment of divine anger — Yahweh's wrath is praised throughout the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, while James 1:20 specifically restricts human anger because it doesn't produce God's righteousness. The implicit move is that anger is appropriate to God but not to humans, which is a coherent theological position but does mean that an emotion presented as virtuous in deity is condemned in humanity. As a contradiction in this entry's framing, the case is weak — Ephesians 4:26 reads more as a regulation of anger than an endorsement, and the texts mostly agree that human anger is dangerous. The contradiction would be sharper if the entry pulled in divine-anger texts as a third pole.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus teach physical resistance?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 5:39 has Jesus teaching non-resistance: do not resist evil, turn the other cheek. Matthew 26:52 has him telling Peter to put away his sword because those who take the sword perish by it. But Luke 22:36 has Jesus instructing his disciples to sell their cloaks and buy swords, and John 2:15 has Jesus himself making a whip of cords and physically driving moneychangers out of the temple. The Jesus of the Sermon on the Mount and the Jesus of the temple cleansing don't appear to operate on the same ethic.
contradictions.commentary: The apologetic harmonizations on this one are unusually creative because the surface contradiction is so visible. For Luke 22:36 — "he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one" — Joel Green in the NICNT Luke and others read it as ironic or symbolic. Jesus is telling them to gear up rhetorically for opposition, not to literally arm themselves, which is why two swords (Luke 22:38) is somehow enough. The problem is that two swords being "enough" only makes sense if the swords are literal, just sufficient for a small defensive band. If the swords were purely symbolic, the disciples wouldn't have presented physical weapons. For John 2:15 — the temple cleansing — apologists often argue that the whip was only used on the animals, not the people. The Greek is genuinely ambiguous (*pantas exebalen* — "he drove them all out" — with *ta te probata kai tous boas* clarifying "both the sheep and the oxen"). D. A. Carson in the Pillar John commentary argues the whip targeted livestock, not humans. But the action is still physical force, and "drove them all out" most naturally includes the merchants. Raymond Brown in the Anchor Bible John takes the violence as directed at moneychangers and merchants, not just animals. So even on the most charitable reading, Jesus uses physical force to expel humans from a religious space. The non-resistance teaching in Matthew 5:39 is also widely understood by critical scholars (Dale Allison, John Meier) as referring to personal honor-disputes — slaps to the face are insults, not lethal attacks — rather than a comprehensive pacifism. So both ends of the contradiction get qualified: the resistance teaching may be narrower than absolute pacifism, and the swords/whip incidents may be narrower than general endorsements of violence. But the contradiction persists. The Sermon on the Mount Jesus and the temple-cleansing Jesus represent two streams of tradition about how Jesus related to coercive force, and the harmonizations work only if you let each text qualify the other rather than letting either stand at full strength.

contradictions.question: Should you fear death?
contradictions.summary: Luke 12:4 has Jesus telling his disciples not to fear those who can kill the body, because they have no more power beyond that. John 7:1 then describes Jesus himself avoiding Judea "because the Jews sought to kill him." The teacher who tells his followers not to fear death-threats appears to behave as though he himself takes them seriously enough to avoid the region where the threat is greatest.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of those contradictions that depends entirely on the difference between teaching and behavior, and the apologetic response is reasonable but not airtight. Standard harmonizations from D. A. Carson in the Pillar John and Andreas Köstenberger in the BECNT John argue that Jesus's avoidance of Judea was not fear-driven but strategically timed — he wasn't running from death, he was managing the timeline of his own approach to the cross. The Johannine "hour" (cf. John 7:6, 7:8, 7:30) is a recurring motif throughout John's Gospel: Jesus operates on a divinely-ordained schedule, and premature confrontation with Jerusalem would short-circuit the passion narrative. On this reading, John 7:1 isn't reporting fear, it's reporting tactical patience. That's a coherent Johannine theological reading and it preserves the consistency between Jesus's teaching and behavior. But it's also a reading that depends on theological commitments the synoptic Jesus may not share. In Mark, Jesus's approach to Jerusalem reads more as deliberate confrontation than carefully-timed self-preservation, and the Gethsemane prayer ("let this cup pass from me," Mark 14:36) suggests an authentic moment of dread about death — which is itself in tension with Luke 12:4's teaching. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* treats Gethsemane as preserving genuine Jesus-tradition about anxiety in the face of death. So the contradiction isn't only between John 7:1 and Luke 12:4 — it runs deeper, between the Lukan teaching of fearlessness and the broader synoptic and Johannine portrayal of a Jesus who is at minimum strategic about death and at moments visibly distressed by it. The harmonization works if you accept the Johannine "hour" theology as the controlling frame; it gets messier if you take the synoptic data alongside. As a contradiction this is real but the resolution is closer than the database wording suggests — John 7:1 isn't necessarily about fear, but the broader question "did Jesus practice what he taught about not fearing death" gets harder when Gethsemane is included.
